body: His mother never wrote it down, which is why the thing with the pan is being done badly, by a man in his forties, in a small kitchen with the extractor fan going on the afternoon before the feast. His daughter is fourteen and is laying the table because she has been asked twice. He puts music on from his phone — the same recording he has put on for this afternoon every year since he was a student, scratchy, and old when he was born. Somewhere in the second verse he realises she is singing along under her breath. She cannot order a coffee in that language. She has every word of that song.

Neither of them treated that as an event, and it was one. Something crossed from one generation to the next in a kitchen, without a lesson and without anybody deciding to keep it up, on an ordinary Thursday that happened to have a date on it.

Migration erodes in a predictable order, and anybody in the second or third generation can watch it in their own family. The language goes first, usually within two generations. The food lasts longer because it is daily. The music lasts longest of all, and what preserves it is the calendar.

It is worth being precise about why the calendar does that work, because the mechanism is not sentiment. A date is a machine for repetition. It comes round whether or not the parents kept up the classes, whether or not the family still lives near enough to gather. Nobody has to remember to hold the feast, because the year holds it for them, and whatever is attached to that date gets replayed on schedule for as long as the date is kept at all. Attach a song to a Thursday and it dies with the habit. Attach it to a feast and it survives the habit, the move, the language and usually the person who first put it on.
The dial this article ends at carries 121 stations between HM 300.30 and HM 398.70, 40 of them international, across 29 languages. Each language holds its own frequency, hosts and hours.

Which gives holiday programming a job far larger than atmosphere, and makes it expensive to do properly. A grandchild who cannot hold a conversation in the language will still know every word of the song that gets sung once a year, and for a great many families that once-a-year airing is the entire transfer — the one point in the year when the older repertoire is audible in a house that otherwise runs completely in the new country’s music. Programme it lazily and you have not merely made a dull hour. You have missed the only appointment that song had in anybody’s year.

Lazy is also the default, because there is a globally famous version of nearly everything now. The same recordings play in the same shops in every city on earth for six weeks, and they are good recordings, sung beautifully by people who deserve their fame. What they quietly do is stand in the doorway. A family reaching for the season finds them first, and the version the grandmother sang — thinner, odder, with a verse nobody outside one region learned — is not competing on equal terms. It is not rejected. It is never reached for, which over three decades comes to the same thing.

The arrangement of this band is meant to make that harder. Each language sits on its own number rather than sharing one, hosted in that language rather than translated into it afterwards, running on its own clock. December therefore does not sound the same across the dial, and is not supposed to. Whatever a season sounds like in one language is what that frequency plays, and the number does not move from year to year — which is the property a calendar needs to do anything at all.
So the question for a holiday station is not whether the music is good. It is whose version of the season is in the room.

The obvious objection is that none of this is scarce any more. Everything ever recorded is a search away, and a family that wants the old carols can have them in eleven seconds — true, and one of the better things about the age. But searching has a prerequisite nobody notices until it is gone. You have to know what you are looking for: the title, or a line of it, or at minimum that such a song exists and belonged to you. That is exactly the knowledge the second generation loses first, and no search box recovers it, because a search box only answers the question it is asked. What a broadcast can do, and a library cannot, is put a song in front of somebody who had no idea it was theirs.
Nobody searches for a song they have forgotten the name of.

There is a house on the north-west side of Chicago where the table gets laid on the twenty-fourth of December and the radio goes on at about four, before anyone arrives, while the grandmother works through the fish. Her Polish is the Polish of a town that no longer sounds like that, and her grandsons speak enough to be polite. Around six one of the old carols comes on, one with a lot of verses that goes at walking pace, and she does not stop what she is doing; she sings it at the sink with her back to the room. The younger boy is nineteen and has his phone out under the table, and he is not scrolling. He is typing in the first line to find out what it is called.

That is the transfer, and notice what it took. Not a class, not an appeal to heritage, not the boy deciding to be interested. It took the song playing in the room he was already in, on the one day of the year he was certain to be in it.

There is a cost and it should be said plainly. Old repertoire is uneven. A lot of it was recorded badly, in halls with poor acoustics, by choirs who were not paid. Some is sentimental in ways that are hard to defend, and some is simply worse than the famous version, which got famous partly by being better. And it can hurt. A song from the old country at the wrong moment can put a person on the floor of their own kitchen, because it arrives carrying everybody who used to be at that table.

None of which is an argument for a smoother season. It is very nearly the argument for this one. The famous recordings are pleasant precisely because they belong to nobody in particular, and a thing that belongs to nobody can neither cost you anything nor give you anything. The old carol is rough because it came from a real place with real people in it, and the reason it can take the breath out of a woman at a sink is the same reason a nineteen-year-old wants to know what it is called.

So the claim is narrow. Holidays are where the old country survives, not because families turn devout in December but because a date is the only thing left in a scattered life that recurs on its own. What plays on those days does the work that language lessons, good intentions and photograph albums were all asked to do and mostly failed at. It is worth choosing on purpose, and worth it being the real thing rather than the international edition of the season.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there. There is music, which is most of it — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running where the children are. And there is the international band, hosted in its own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, each language on its own frequency and hours. 46 stations are on air, and there is no menu to work through before something starts.

If the old country in your family is Poland, start at HM 325.40 — Polska Inspire. It is the Polish-language flagship of the band, and the right recommendation here because of what it carries: Catholic devotional heritage alongside modern Polish worship — both halves of what a Polish house actually sings, rather than the famous versions with Polish words fitted to them. It keeps Polish hours, Poranna Chwała in the morning and Wieczorne Uwielbienie at night, and it is on air on the twenty-fourth of December whether or not anybody in Chicago remembered to look for anything. If your old country is somewhere else, the band holds 40 international frequencies and the argument is identical; only the number changes.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which languages people are really reaching for — which is how the next language edition, and the next holiday schedule, get built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Put HM 325.40 on at four on the day your family keeps, before anybody arrives, and leave it running while you cook. Do not explain it and do not make it a project. The person it will reach is not the one who chose it. It is whoever happens to be laying the table when the long carol comes round.
